$comment: Bibliography for muscle records. `key` is cited from data/muscles-*.json. `notes` points at the reading notes in papers/ (tracked); `pdf` names the local PDF (git-ignored).

sources.authors: Abdala V, Diogo R
sources.title: Comparative anatomy, homologies and evolution of the pectoral and forelimb musculature of tetrapods with special attention to extant limbed amphibians and reptiles
sources.role: Primary source for the pectoral/forelimb homology matrix (their Tables 1–3) across Caudata, Anura, Testudines, Lepidosauria, Crocodylia, Aves.

sources.authors: Abrahão VP, Shibatta OA
sources.title: Gross morphology of the brain of Pseudopimelodus bufonius (Siluriformes: Pseudopimelodidae)
sources.role: OUT OF SCOPE for this dataset — catfish brain morphology, no skeletal muscle content. Listed so the papers/ folder is fully accounted for.

sources.authors: Allen V, Molnar J, Parker W, Pollard A, Nolan G, Hutchinson JR
sources.title: Comparative architectural properties of limb muscles in Crocodylidae and Alligatoridae and their relevance to divergent use of asymmetrical gaits
sources.role: Crocodylian limb muscle architecture and attachment data.

sources.authors: Allen VR, Kilbourne BM, Hutchinson JR
sources.title: The evolution of pelvic limb muscle moment arms in bird-line archosaurs
sources.role: Crocodylian-to-avian pelvic limb muscle homology table (their Table 1, 25 correspondences) plus 13 three-dimensional musculoskeletal models spanning Marasuchus to extant birds. Primary source for avian hindlimb nomenclature here, and the methodological model for turning attachment records into moment arms on fossils.

sources.authors: Anderson PSL
sources.title: Cranial muscle homology across modern gnathostomes
sources.journal: Biological Journal of the Linnean Society
sources.role: A cross-gnathostome cranial nomenclature reconciliation, written against exactly the terminological confusion this dataset is keyed to dissolve.

sources.authors: Bauer WJ
sources.title: A contribution to the morphology of visceral jaw-opening muscles of urodeles (Amphibia: Caudata)
sources.role: Depressor mandibulae and ceratomandibularis across larval, neotenic and metamorphosed urodeles. The facial-nerve jaw openers, which is the half of the salamander cranial series Ziermann & Diogo's development paper does not resolve.

sources.authors: Bishop PJ, Pierce SE
sources.title: Late acquisition of erect hindlimb posture and function in the forerunners of therian mammals
sources.role: Stem-synapsid hindlimb muscle reconstruction and posture inference.

sources.authors: Blotto BL, Pereyra MO, Grant T, Faivovich J
sources.title: Hand and foot musculature of Anura: structure, homology, terminology, and synapomorphies for major clades
sources.journal: Bulletin of the American Museum of Natural History 443: 1–156
sources.role: 156-page monograph on anuran hand and foot musculature with explicit homology and terminology sections. The dedicated autopod source the gap analysis called for.

sources.authors: Bodenham EH, Spiekman SNF, Maidment SCR, Upchurch P, Mannion PD
sources.title: A second species of non-crocodyliform crocodylomorph from the Late Triassic fissure deposits of southwestern UK: implications for locomotory ecological diversity in Saltoposuchidae
sources.role: Describes Galahadosuchus jonesi (NHMUK PV R 10002), a saltoposuchid from Cromhall Quarry, and is the first source in this dataset for the stem-crocodylomorph column. Osteological rather than myological, but it identifies the muscle-bearing correlates on the coracoid and femur and compares them directly with Dromicosuchus (NCSM 13733) and Terrestrisuchus, which is what makes the sphenosuchian grade scoreable at all.

sources.authors: Borczyk B, Skawiński T
sources.title: Variation in the jaw musculature of ratsnakes and their allies (Serpentes: Colubridae)
sources.role: Colubrid jaw musculature and its variation. Snakes are absent from this dataset as occurrences, and Johnston (2014) — whose folded-sheet model the adductor records rest on — dissected ten snakes and no lizard, so this is the group his primary evidence actually came from.

sources.authors: Boumans MLLM, Krings M, Wagner H
sources.title: Muscular arrangement and muscle attachment sites in the cervical region of the American barn owl (Tyto furcata pratincola)
sources.role: Nine cervical muscles of a barn owl with origin and insertion tabulated per muscle (their Table 3) across fourteen cervical vertebrae. The avian neck at vertebra-by-vertebra resolution, against an axial column here that carries whole tracts.

sources.authors: Burch SH
sources.title: Complete forelimb myology of the basal theropod dinosaur Tawa hallae based on a novel robust muscle reconstruction method
sources.role: Complete forelimb myology of a Late Triassic basal theropod, reconstructed on the extant phylogenetic bracket with explicit Level I/II/III inference — the same confidence vocabulary Molnar & Diogo (2021) supply and Molnar et al. (2018) use on the tetrapod stem. 293 attachment statements in 27 pages. **Scored**: the `theropoda-stem` taxon it needed is in taxa.json and 35 of its muscles are in the dataset, which is the whole of the avian half of the archosaur stem. Its value beyond the rows is that it argues with its own sources in print — against Jasinoski et al. (2006) on the deltoid origins, the supracoracoideus and the presence of coracobrachialis longus, against Diogo & Abdala (2010) on the homology of the avian deltoideus minor and ulnimetacarpalis dorsalis, and against Meers (2003) on which crocodylian muscle carries which name. Those disagreements are recorded in the attachmentNotes rather than resolved.

sources.authors: Campbell KHS
sources.title: Rat dissection guide
sources.role: Laboratory dissection vocabulary for the rat. Not evidence of homology, but the names students read off the bench — the register the dataset was missing, which is why clavotrapezius, acromiodeltoid and spinodeltoid matched nothing.

sources.authors: Chen A, Steell EM, Benson RBJ, Field DJ
sources.title: Toward a comprehensive anatomical matrix for crown birds: phylogenetic insights from the pectoral girdle and forelimb skeleton
sources.role: Osteological character matrix for the crown-bird pectoral girdle and forelimb. Skeletal rather than myological, but it is the model for how a character matrix over this anatomy is built and scored — directly relevant to the phylogeny view.

sources.authors: Cieri RL
sources.title: The axial anatomy of monitor lizards (Varanidae)
sources.role: Squamate axial musculature and its regionalisation; the lepidosaur column for the axial records.

sources.authors: Clack JA, Fay RR, Popper AN (eds)
sources.title: Evolution of the Vertebrate Ear: Evidence from the Fossil Record
sources.role: Edited volume on ear evolution. Background for the hyomandibula-to-stapes transformation and the stapedius; not yet mined for individual records.

sources.authors: Cole NJ, Hall TE, Don EK, Berger S, Boisvert CA, Neyt C, Ericsson R, Joss J, Gurevich DB, Currie PD
sources.title: Development and evolution of the muscles of the pelvic fin
sources.role: Developmental evidence for how pelvic fin muscle is built, across the fish-tetrapod transition. Developmental origin is the decisive homology evidence the schema asks for and the fin records mostly lack.

sources.authors: Collings AJ, Richards CT
sources.title: Digital dissection of the pelvis and hindlimb of the red-legged running frog, Phlyctimantis maculatus, using diffusible iodine-based contrast-enhanced computed tomography (DICE µCT)
sources.role: Attachment-level anuran pelvis and hindlimb from contrast CT. Anura is scored at 23%, and this is a walking rather than jumping frog, so it is not the Rana-shaped default. Recorded here as Kassina maculata until now; the paper itself uses Phlyctimantis maculatus, the genus having been moved.

sources.authors: Cuff AR, Wiseman ALA, Bishop PJ, Michel KB, Hutchinson JR
sources.title: Anatomically grounded estimation of hindlimb muscle sizes in Archosauria
sources.role: Method for estimating muscle size from attachment area in archosaurs. Directly addresses what Leavey et al. warn about — that a correlate locates an attachment but does not size the muscle.

sources.authors: Dearden RP, Mansuit R, Cuckovic A, Herrel A, Didier D, Tafforeau P, Pradel A
sources.title: The morphology and evolution of chondrichthyan cranial muscles: a digital dissection of the elephantfish Callorhinchus milii and the catshark Scyliorhinus canicula
sources.role: Chondrichthyan cranial muscles from synchrotron tomography, covering both a holocephalan and an elasmobranch. Preprint version; a peer-reviewed version was published subsequently and should replace this entry once checked.

sources.authors: Demuth OE, Wiseman ALA, et al.
sources.title: Three-dimensional polygonal muscle modelling and line of action estimation in living and extinct taxa
sources.role: Method for building 3D muscle volumes and estimating lines of action from skeletal geometry. The methodological bridge from this dataset's attachment records to biomechanical reconstruction.

sources.authors: Demuth OE, Wiseman ALA, Hutchinson JR
sources.title: Quantitative biomechanical assessment of locomotor capabilities of the stem archosaur Euparkeria capensis
sources.role: Muscle reconstruction and locomotor modelling for a stem archosaur. A fossil taxon earlier on the archosaur stem than any column the dataset carries.

sources.authors: Dick TJM, Clemente CJ
sources.title: How to build your dragon: scaling of muscle architecture from the world's smallest to the world's largest monitor lizard
sources.role: Varanid limb muscle architecture across three orders of magnitude in body mass — mass, fascicle length, pennation, PCSA. Named by Mansuit & Herrel (2021) as a key architecture source; the squamate counterpart to Hudson et al. (2011).

sources.authors: Didier D
sources.title: Myology of the pectoral, branchial, and jaw regions of the ratfish Hydrolagus colliei (Holocephali)
sources.role: Holocephalan myology, a chondrichthyan lineage the dataset does not sample at all — the exemplar column is Squalus. An undergraduate honours thesis: treat as a description to check, not as an authority.

sources.authors: Diogo R
sources.title: Comparative anatomy, homologies and evolution of the mandibular, hyoid and hypobranchial muscles of bony fish and tetrapods
sources.role: Arch-by-arch homologies for the osteichthyan cranial series. The direct precursor to the arch scheme the cranial records use.

sources.authors: Diogo R, Abdala V, Lonergan N, Wood BA
sources.title: From fish to modern humans — comparative anatomy, homologies and evolution of the head and neck musculature
sources.role: One head-muscle homology scheme across the whole gnathostome span, with the mandibular, hyoid, branchial and hypobranchial groups named consistently from shark to human.

sources.authors: Diogo R, Wood BA, Aziz MA, Burrows A
sources.title: On the origin, homologies and evolution of primate facial muscles, with a particular focus on hominoids and a suggested unifying nomenclature for the facial muscles of the Mammalia
sources.role: A single nomenclature for the mammalian facial muscles, derived from the hyoid arch and grouped by the branch of the facial nerve that supplies each.

sources.authors: Diogo R, Abdala V
sources.title: Comparative anatomy, homologies and evolution of the pectoral muscles of bony fish and tetrapods
sources.role: The osteichthyan half of the pectoral homology argument that Abdala & Diogo (2010) carries into tetrapods.

sources.authors: Diogo R, Johnston P, Molnar JL, Esteve-Altava B
sources.title: Characteristic tetrapod musculoskeletal limb phenotype emerged more than 400 MYA in basal lobe-finned fishes
sources.role: Primary source for the ancestral fin muscle set and for the Latimeria, Neoceratodus and Polypterus columns. Supplies the one-to-one homology hypotheses linking fish fin muscles to tetrapod limb muscles.

sources.authors: Diogo R, Johnston P, Molnar JL, Esteve-Altava B
sources.title: Supplementary Materials — Tables S1–S7: muscle–bone attachments in Neoceratodus and Latimeria, and pectoral/pelvic homology matrices
sources.role: Tables S1–S4 give per-muscle origin and insertion for the Neoceratodus and Latimeria pectoral and pelvic fins. Source of every fish attachment record here. Local copy at data/raw/diogo-etal-2016-supplementary.docx (git-ignored).

sources.authors: Diogo R, Bello-Hellegouarch G, Kohlsdorf T, Esteve-Altava B, Molnar JL
sources.title: Comparative myology and evolution of marsupials and other vertebrates, with notes on complexity, bauplan, and 'scala naturae'
sources.role: Marsupial myology set against the wider vertebrate pattern. Theria here is scored from placental exemplars — a mustelid, a rat — so this is the source that would tell the column whether its rows are therian or eutherian.

sources.authors: Diogo R, Molnar J
sources.title: Comparative anatomy, evolution, and homologies of tetrapod hindlimb muscles, comparison with forelimb muscles, and deconstruction of the forelimb–hindlimb serial homology hypothesis
sources.role: Primary source for the pelvic/hindlimb homology matrix (their Tables 1–8) and for the critique of forelimb–hindlimb serial homology.

sources.authors: Diogo R, Ziermann JM
sources.title: Muscles of chondrichthyan paired appendages: comparison with osteichthyans, deconstruction of the fore–hindlimb serial homology dogma, and new insights on the evolution of the vertebrate neck
sources.role: Chondrichthyan outgroup condition for paired-appendage muscles.

sources.authors: Ercoli MD, Echarri S, Busker F, Álvarez A, Morales MM, Turazzini GF
sources.title: The functional and phylogenetic implications of the myology of the lumbar region, tail, and hind limbs of the lesser grison (Galictis cuja)
sources.role: The hindlimb, lumbar and tail companion to Ercoli et al. (2014) on the forelimb. Origins and insertions for a therian column currently scored at 15%.

sources.authors: Ercoli MD, Álvarez A, Stefanini MI, Busker F, Morales MM
sources.title: Muscular anatomy of the forelimbs of the lesser grison (Galictis cuja), and a functional and phylogenetic overview of Mustelidae and other Caniformia
sources.role: Therian forelimb attachment and action data, with muscle mass fractions.

sources.authors: Fahn-Lai P, Biewener AA, Pierce SE
sources.title: Broad similarities in shoulder muscle architecture and organization across two amniotes: implications for reconstructing non-mammalian synapsids
sources.role: Direct monotreme–lepidosaur shoulder comparison used for synapsid bracketing.

sources.authors: Fisher HI, Goodman DC
sources.title: The myology of the whooping crane, Grus americana
sources.role: Complete myology of a flying neognath, with an explicit origin and insertion for every muscle across 156 pages. This is the source the avian column has been missing: Aves sits at 13% because its rows cite a synonymy survey, a penguin, a plate atlas and two musculoskeletal models, none of which states an attachment in prose. Scanned and OCRed unevenly: only 83 of ~328 muscle headings carry a recoverable Origin paragraph in the text layer, and plate-facing pages OCR to noise. It cannot be bulk-extracted and must be read page by page against the plates.

sources.authors: Freitas LM, Pereira DKS, Pereira KF, Santos OP, Lima FC
sources.title: Muscular anatomy of the pectoral girdle and forelimb of Iguana i. iguana (Squamata: Iguanidae)
sources.role: Iguanid pectoral and forelimb attachment data. The only source here that dissects Iguana specifically, against a lepidosaur column otherwise built on varanids and Abdala & Diogo's survey.

sources.authors: Fritzsch B
sources.title: Evolution and development of extra-ocular nerves and muscles in vertebrates
sources.role: Extraocular muscle and nerve evolution. NOT peer reviewed — used only as a pointer to primary literature.

sources.authors: Gai Z, Zhu M, Ahlberg PE, Donoghue PCJ
sources.title: The evolution of the spiracular region from jawless fishes to tetrapods
sources.role: Fossil sequence for the spiracular region from jawless fishes to tetrapods; the anatomical basis for treating the spiracular pouch as antecedent to the tympanic cavity.

sources.authors: Gambaryan PP, Aristov AA, Dixon JM, Zubtsova GY
sources.title: Peculiarities of the hind limb musculature in monotremes: an anatomical description and functional approach
sources.role: The monotreme hind limb, dissected in both genera and described separately for each — the companion to the 2015 forelimb monograph.

sources.authors: Regnault S, Pierce SE
sources.title: Pectoral girdle and forelimb musculoskeletal function in the echidna (Tachyglossus aculeatus): insights into mammalian locomotor evolution
sources.role: A musculoskeletal model of the echidna shoulder and forelimb — moment arms rather than attachments.

sources.authors: Gambaryan PP, Kuznetsov AN, Panyutina AA, Gerasimov SV
sources.title: Shoulder girdle and forelimb myology of extant Monotremata
sources.role: Monotreme attachment data — the intermediate condition between the reptilian and therian pectoral girdle.

sources.authors: Gest TR
sources.title: Medical Gross Anatomy — Anatomy Tables: muscles
sources.journal: Teaching resource (web), Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center
sources.role:
Origin, insertion, action, innervation and arterial supply for 279 HUMAN muscles across seven regions, in one table. **The human column runs on this**, and the column exists to be a baseline: it is the anatomy most readers already carry, and every other column in the dataset can be read against it. It is also the densest source here by rows per page.

Dissection-derived, and treated as such — the human body is the most dissected animal there has ever been, so these attachments rest on a larger sample than any single-specimen description in this corpus. It describes one animal and makes no cross-taxon homology claims, so it carries no `homologyScope`, exactly as Cunningham (1882) and Osawa (1898) do not; where a later comparative treatment homologises differently that treatment governs the homology and this one still governs the attachment.

Web resource with no archived snapshot held, so the rows in `data/` are the only in-repo record of it. Its rows are paraphrased, never copied.

sources.authors: Ghetie V, Chitescu St, Cotofan V, Hillebrand A
sources.title: Anatomical atlas of domestic birds / Atlas de anatomie a pasarilor domestice
sources.role: Plate atlas of the domestic fowl, duck and goose in four languages. **Carries no descriptive myology**: a density check over the full extraction finds zero origin or insertion statements in 154 pages — the anatomy is in labelled figures, not in prose. It is a source for names and for what a structure looks like, not for attachments, and it is the reason the *Gallus* column cannot be closed from the corpus as it stands. Rows that cite it for an attachment are citing the wrong kind of book; one such row on the latissimus dorsi has been corrected.

sources.authors: Godoy PL, Bronzati M, Eltink E, Marsola JCA, Cidade GM, Langer MC, Montefeltro FC
sources.title: Postcranial anatomy of Pissarrachampsa sera (Crocodyliformes, Baurusuchidae) from the Late Cretaceous of Brazil: insights on lifestyle and phylogenetic significance
sources.role: Labels muscle scars directly on the described elements — biceps and humeroradialis insertion tubercles on the radius, triceps scars and a pronator quadratus origin fossa on the ulna, iliotibialis rugosities on the supraacetabular crest. Osteological correlates on a crocodyliform, which is the grade between the sphenosuchians and the crown.

sources.authors: Günther A
sources.title: Contribution to the anatomy of Hatteria (Rhynchocephalus, Owen)
sources.journal: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London 157:595-629
sources.role:
The first anatomical description of the tuatara, and the paper every later account cites first. A whole-animal memoir — skeleton, limb musculature, integuments, sense organs, viscera — 42 pages including three plates, not a systematic myology. 119 mentions of muscle across 54 attachment statements.

**Its value is partly what it says about naming.** Günther argues that the muscular system of the lizard limb is characterised by partial confluence of the fascicles and tendons of different muscles and by loose connection of the fascicles generally, and warns against being tempted into a nomenclature created for higher vertebrates with more diversified limb action. That is the same problem this dataset exists to hold, stated in 1867.

Acquired from archive.org, which became reachable from this environment between two mining passes. **The item that turns up first for this title — `philtrans07125835` — is a three-page abstract from the Proceedings whose first page is a different author on corals**; the memoir itself is in `philosophicaltra1571roya`, Phil. Trans. vol. 157, at printed pp. 595-629 (PDF pages 667-708 with plates).

sources.authors: Gyambibi A, Lemelin P
sources.title: Comparative and quantitative myology of the forearm and hand of prosimian primates
sources.role: Strepsirrhine forearm and hand with muscle mass data. Quantitative, so it carries architecture as well as attachment, and it is a grasping rather than a cursorial or digging hand.

sources.authors: Haas G
sources.title: Muscles of the jaws and associated structures in the Rhynchocephalia and Squamata
sources.journal: Biology of the Reptilia 4 (Morphology D), pp. 285-490. Academic Press
sources.role:
**The Sphenodon description this corpus did not have.** Section II is Rhynchocephalia, and its 21 pages of muscle description are the tuatara jaw musculature at the level of detail the dataset scores — adductor mandibulae externus in three layers, levator and retractor anguli oris, pterygoideus, depressor mandibulae, constrictor colli, ceratomandibularis, levator bulbi. Haas dissected two specimens himself, in Basel and London, and adjudicates between Lakjer (1926), Luther, Poglayen-Neuwall (1953) and Frazzetta where they disagree — including on whether Sphenodon has a levator anguli oris at all, which Lakjer missed and Luther, editing him, put back.

It bears directly on the `levator-anguli-oris` record, whose identification this dataset already calls the crux of the lizard-snake problem: Haas reports that in *Sphenodon* the insertion is the same as in lizards but the origin has not yet shifted to the upper temporal arch, and that the tuatara is the only living animal with two temporal arches in which the lower one gives origin to any adductor. Acquired from the Gans Collections and Charitable Fund's free release; only the Rhynchocephalia section and the synonymy list were fetched, not the 200 pages on Squamata and Ophidia.

sources.authors: Hattori S, Tsuihiji T
sources.title: Homology and osteological correlates of pedal muscles among extant sauropsids
sources.role: Pedal musculature across Lepidosauria, Testudines, Crocodylia and Aves, with osteological correlates named for over 80% of muscles examined. Proposes a major revision to the Romer (1923-27) homology framework for the anterior tibial muscles.

sources.authors: Higashiyama H, Hirasawa T, Oisi Y, Sugahara F, Hyodo S, Kanai Y, Kuratani S
sources.title: On the vagal cardiac nerves, with special reference to the early evolution of the head–trunk interface
sources.role: Vagal innervation and the head–trunk boundary; complements Sefton et al. (2016) on where branchiomeric territory ends.

sources.authors: Huber DR, Soares MC, de Carvalho MR
sources.title: Cranial muscles of chondrichthyans
sources.role: Reference summary of chondrichthyan cranial musculature. Chondrichthyes is the thinnest scored column in the dataset at 5%.

sources.authors: Hudson PE, Corr SA, Payne-Davis RC, Clancy SN, Lane E, Wilson AM
sources.title: Functional anatomy of the cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) forelimb
sources.role: Muscle mass, fascicle length, pennation angle and PCSA for the cheetah forelimb, with greyhound comparison. First architecture data in this dataset.

sources.authors: Hudson PE, Corr SA, Payne-Davis RC, Clancy SN, Lane E, Wilson AM
sources.title: Functional anatomy of the cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) hindlimb
sources.role: Architecture data for the cheetah hindlimb, same protocol as the forelimb paper.

sources.authors: Hutchinson JR, Rankin JW, Rubenson J, Rosenbluth KH, Siston RA, Delp SL
sources.title: Musculoskeletal modelling of an ostrich (Struthio camelus) pelvic limb: influence of limb orientation on muscular capacity during locomotion
sources.role: Thirty-six-muscle three-dimensional model of the ostrich pelvic limb, with mass, fascicle length, pennation angle and maximum isometric force per muscle. First avian architecture data in this dataset.

sources.authors: Huynen L, et al.
sources.title: Reconstruction and in vivo analysis of the extinct tbx5 gene from ancient wingless moa (Aves: Dinornithiformes)
sources.role: Ancient-DNA reconstruction of moa tbx5. Relevant to forelimb identity and reduction; no muscle-level data, so cited as background rather than used in records.

sources.authors: Jacob J, Pescatore T
sources.title: Avian muscular system (ASC-204)
sources.journal: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension Service
sources.role: Poultry-industry summary of avian muscle. Included for completeness; carries no attachment or homology detail the avian records can use.

sources.authors: Jayaram KC, Dhanze JR, Singh R
sources.title: Comparative morphology of the cranial muscles in some species of the genus Arius, with a note on their utility in taxonomy (Ariidae: Siluriformes)
sources.journal: Bulletin of the Zoological Survey of India 5(1): 107–111
sources.role: Mandibular and hyoid muscle complexes in three Arius species. Actinopterygian cranial myology at species resolution; useful for the arch-1 and arch-2 records where the fish columns are currently thin.

sources.authors: Johnston P
sources.title: Cranial muscles of the anurans Leiopelma hochstetteri and Ascaphus truei and the homologies of the mandibular adductors in Lissamphibia and other gnathostomes
sources.role: Origin of the folded-sheet model of the jaw adductor complex. Source for splitting the adductor mandibulae into internus, longus, externus, lateralis and posterior, and for the levator anguli oris.

sources.authors: Johnston P
sources.title: Homology of the jaw muscles in lizards and snakes — a solution from a comparative gnathostome approach
sources.role: Extends the folded-sheet model across Squamata and resolves the lizard–snake jaw adductor problem. Argues insertion position beats trigeminal branch position as the homology criterion.

sources.authors: Jones MEH, Button DJ, Barrett PM, Porro LB
sources.title: Digital dissection of the head of the rock dove (Columba livia) using contrast-enhanced computed tomography
sources.role: Avian cranial muscles, nerves and sense organs from contrast CT. Aves is the second-thinnest column at 13% and has no cranial attachment data at all.

sources.authors: Kępa M, Tomańska A, Staszewska J, Tarnowska M, Klećkowska-Nawrot J, Goździewska-Harłajczuk K, Kuźniarski A, Gębarowski T, Janeczek M
sources.title: Functional anatomy of the thoracic limb of the Komodo dragon (Varanus komodoensis)
sources.role: Varanid forelimb myology. Companion to Tomańska et al. (2025) on the hindlimb and (2024) on the tail — three separate papers from overlapping author groups, all recorded here.

sources.authors: Klinkhamer AJ, Wilhite DR, White MA, Wroe S
sources.title: Digital dissection and three-dimensional interactive models of limb musculature in the Australian estuarine crocodile (Crocodylus porosus)
sources.role: CT plus MRI, with fresh dissection, of two sub-adult Crocodylus porosus — NOT contrast-enhanced CT, which the authors state was not possible at this specimen size. Gives an origin and an insertion for most limb muscles segmented. The main filler of the crocodylian attachment column, and the source of most crocodylian `side` values, since it states an explicit aspect (proximo-lateral, ventro-lateral, medio-posterior) for each attachment. Caveat before scoring from it: trapezius, latissimus dorsi, rhomboideus and serratus ventralis cervicis were destroyed in skinning and their absence here is not an absence in the animal, and insertions described only as 'into the manus/pes' are severed, not coarse.

sources.authors: Leavey A, et al.
sources.title: Comparative muscle anatomy of the anuran pelvis and hindlimb in relation to locomotor mode
sources.role: diceCT digital dissection of the pelvis and hindlimb in 30 frog species across five locomotor modes — the largest digital comparative musculoskeletal analysis in any vertebrate clade. Reports that bone lengths and pelvic crest sizes are generally NOT reliable predictors of muscle size, and finds many-to-one form-function mapping.

sources.authors: Lemelin P, Diogo R
sources.title: Anatomy, function, and evolution of the primate hand musculature
sources.journal: In: Kivell TL et al. (eds), The Evolution of the Primate Hand (Springer)
sources.role: Review of primate hand musculature and its homologies. The hand is the second-thinnest region here at 36%, and this chapter is the one source that treats the intrinsic hand muscles as a homology problem rather than a list.

sources.authors: Lemell P, Lemell C, Snelderwaard P, Gumpenberger M, Wochesländer R, Weisgram J
sources.title: Feeding patterns of Chelus fimbriatus (Pleurodira: Chelidae)
sources.role: Suction-feeding kinematics in a pleurodire. Function rather than myology: useful for what the turtle hyobranchial apparatus does, not for scoring attachments.

sources.authors: Liparini A, Schultz CL
sources.title: A reconstruction of the thigh musculature of the extinct pseudosuchian Prestosuchus chiniquensis from the Dinodontosaurus Assemblage Zone (Middle Triassic), southern Brazil
sources.role: Thigh-muscle reconstruction for Prestosuchus under explicit Witmer inference levels. The first source here for the loricatan grade. Its two-column layout interleaves badly on text extraction, so only the claims verified against surrounding context are scored; the rest of the reconstruction is still to be mined by hand.

sources.authors: Lőw P, Molnár K, Kriska G
sources.title: Dissection of a frog (Rana sp.), in Atlas of Animal Anatomy and Histology
sources.role: Laboratory dissection vocabulary for Rana. Same register as the rat and mustelid guides, for the anuran column.

sources.authors: Lowie A, De Kegel B, Wilkinson M, Measey J, O'Reilly JC, Kley NJ, Gaucher P, Brecko J, Kleinteich T, Van Hoorebeke L, Herrel A
sources.title: Does the morphology of the forelimb flexor muscles differ between lizards using different habitats?
sources.role: Forelimb flexor morphology across lizards of different habitats. Lepidosauria's forearm is its largest remaining gap at 8 unscored rows, and this is the only source here aimed squarely at it.

sources.authors: Mansuit R, Herrel A
sources.title: The evolution of appendicular muscles during the fin-to-limb transition: possible insights through studies of soft tissues, a perspective
sources.role: Muscle architecture (mass, PCSA) across the fin-to-limb transition, binned into the four abductor/adductor × superficialis/profundus groups. A Perspective piece; its own data are a literature meta-analysis, not new dissection.

sources.authors: Martins A, Passos P, Pinto R
sources.title: Moving beyond the surface: comparative head and neck myology of threadsnakes (Epictinae, Leptotyphlopidae, Serpentes), with comments on the 'scolecophidian' muscular system
sources.role: Head and neck myology across 18 threadsnake species with per-species origin and insertion in supplementary tables. Caution: scolecophidians are miniaturised burrowers with heavily modified skulls, so these are not a stand-in for the lepidosaur column, whose exemplars are Timon and varanids. Best used for what varies within Squamata rather than to fill Lepidosauria rows.

sources.authors: Mathou A, Bonnet X, Daoues K, Ksas R, Herrel A
sources.title: Evolutionary convergence of muscle architecture in relation to locomotor ecology in snakes
sources.role: Axial muscle architecture across snakes of different locomotor ecologies. Architecture for the axial column, which has none, in the limbless lepidosaurs the dataset does not otherwise reach.

sources.authors: Matsuoka H, Hasegawa Y
sources.title: Myology and osteology of the Whooper Swan Cygnus cygnus (Aves: Anatidae). Part 1. Muscles attached to the sternum, coracoid, clavicle, scapula and humerus
sources.journal: Bulletin of the Gunma Museum of Natural History 11: 7–14
sources.role: Myology and osteology of one old male whooper swan, GMNH-VA-04-02, written explicitly for palaeontologists: the authors state that published avian myology does not let you identify which structure on a bone carries which muscle, and answer it by figuring and numbering every attachment site on the sternum, coracoid, clavicle, scapula and humerus. **The highest attachment-statement density in the bibliography** — twelve pages, 22 scored rows. Part 1 only, so several muscles are recorded with an origin and no insertion; that is scope, not omission, and the rows say so.

sources.authors: McKitrick MC
sources.title: Forelimb myology of loons (Gaviiformes), with comments on the relationship of loons and tubenoses (Procellariiformes)
sources.journal: Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society
sources.role: Loon forelimb myology with descriptions and illustrations, used phylogenetically. A third neognath forelimb against the crane and the tinamou, and one from a foot-propelled diver rather than a generalised flier.

sources.authors: Meers MB
sources.title: Crocodylian forelimb musculature and its relevance to Archosauria
sources.role: One of the six naming schemes Abdala & Diogo's Tables 1-3 exist to translate between, and until now the only one not held here in full. Crocodylian forelimb attachments with archosaur reconstruction in view.

sources.authors: Miyashita T
sources.title: Fishing for jaws in early vertebrate evolution: a new hypothesis of mandibular confinement
sources.role: Hypothesis for the origin of the jaw. Background for the mandibular-arch records and for why cyclostome feeding muscles are not homologised with the gnathostome adductor complex.

sources.authors: Molnar JL, Diogo R
sources.title: Evolution, homology, and development of tetrapod limb muscles
sources.role: Review of methods and confidence levels for reconstructing muscles in fossils; source of the confidence vocabulary used here.

sources.authors: Molnar JL, Diaz RE Jr, Skorka T, Dagliyan G, Diogo R
sources.title: Comparative musculoskeletal anatomy of chameleon limbs, with implications for the evolution of arboreal locomotion in lizards and for teratology
sources.role: Squamate limb muscle attachments in a derived arboreal grasping form.

sources.authors: Molnar JL, Diogo R, Hutchinson JR, Pierce SE
sources.title: Reconstructing pectoral appendicular muscle anatomy in fossil fish and tetrapods over the fins-to-limbs transition
sources.role: Fin-to-limb polarity: which pectoral muscles were present in sarcopterygian fish, which appeared at tetrapodomorph and crown-tetrapod nodes.

sources.authors: Naumann B, Warth P, Olsson L, Konstantinidis P
sources.title: The development of the cucullaris muscle and the branchial musculature in the Longnose Gar
sources.role: Actinopterygian developmental data on cucullaris and branchial muscle origin.

sources.authors: Navarro EA, Quipildor M, Quinteros S
sources.title: Description of the neuroanatomy of the brachial plexus in South American lizards. Phylogenetic implications
sources.role: Squamate brachial plexus composition — the innervation backbone for lepidosaur forelimb records.

sources.authors: Omura A, Anzai W, Endo H
sources.title: Functional and morphological variety in trunk muscles of Urodela
sources.role: Trunk musculature across five salamanders of three habitat types, INCLUDING Necturus maculosus. The only source here that scores the axial column of the animal most often on the dissection bench.

sources.authors: O'Reilly JC, Summers AP, Ritter DA
sources.title: The evolution of the functional role of trunk muscles during locomotion in adult amphibians
sources.role: Function of the lissamphibian trunk musculature in locomotion. Frames what the axial records are FOR, against a region scored at 24%.

sources.authors: Osawa G
sources.title: Beiträge zur Anatomie der Hatteria punctata
sources.role:
**The tuatara myology the corpus was missing.** 211 pages in German with 53 text figures, in three parts: Zur Knochenlehre (osteology), **Zur Muskellehre**, and Zur Nervenlehre. The myology is systematic and numbered, organised by layer (`Schicht`) — capiti-dorso-clavicularis, levator scapulae, collo-scapularis, pectoralis, supracoracoideus, subscapulo-coraco-brachialis, coraco-antibrachialis, anconaeus, then the muscles of the palm and dorsum of the hand, then the hindlimb from gastrocnemius through tibialis posticus and anticus to abductor et extensor hallucis longus. 406 mentions of Muskel, 151 attachment statements.

It covers the **limbs**, which Haas (1973) does not, so the two together are a whole tuatara. The nerve section describes the brachial plexus muscle by muscle, which is the only source in this bibliography that could put structured `nerves` on a lepidosaur row.

**Mined: 62 rows, taking the tuatara from 11 to 73.** The translation pass it needed is done; the bridging was the harder half — the attachment vocabulary is Ursprung/Ansatz/entspringt rather than origin/insertion, and the muscle names are Osawa's own compounds rather than the Romerian scheme the rest of the dataset uses. Acquired from archive.org: Archiv f. mikr. Anat. Bd. 51, printed pp. 481-691 (PDF pages 495-705).

sources.authors: Bock J, King A, Honea S
sources.title: Salmonid anatomy and dissection workshop handbook
sources.journal: Oregon State University Klamath Basin Research & Extension Center
sources.role: Laboratory dissection vocabulary for a salmonid. Teaching material rather than comparative myology; the actinopterygian records rest on Winterbottom and Diogo.

sources.authors: Pereyra ME, Bona P, Cerda IA, Desántolo B
sources.title: Osteohistological correlates of muscular attachment in terrestrial and freshwater Testudines
sources.role: Pectoral girdle and forelimb attachment sites in Chelonoidis chilensis, Phrynops hilarii and Hydromedusa tectifera, examined in thin section. Density check on the PDF: 85 origin/insertion mentions in 15,000 words, so this is NOT a descriptive myology and will not fill Testudines rows. Its value is the other half — it classifies Sharpey's fibre orientation at each attachment into three patterns and ties them to the muscle, which is direct evidence for what the `correlate` flag asserts and the entry point for the 18 flagged correlates in GAPS §3 that carry no muscle. Mine it for correlates, not for attachments.

sources.authors: Pereyra ME, Cerroni MA, Lecuona A, Bona P, Fernández Dumont ML, Otero A
sources.title: Hindlimb and pelvic anatomy of Caiman yacare (Archosauria, Pseudosuchia): myology and osteological correlates with emphasis on lower leg and autopodial musculature
sources.role: Crocodylian crural and pedal myology in seven layers, with osteological correlates. The authors identify bony correlates for PEDAL muscles for the first time — fine striations on metatarsal surfaces — and report that most correlates vary little between crocodylian species, which is what makes them usable on fossils. Fetched from PubMed Central (green OA); no local PDF.

sources.authors: Přikryl T, Aerts P, Havelková P, Herrel A, Roček Z
sources.title: Pelvic and thigh musculature in frogs (Anura) and origin of anuran jumping locomotion
sources.role: Anuran pelvic and thigh musculature with, for each muscle, the competing identifications of earlier authors in brackets. Primary source for the anuran letter-code nomenclature that Diogo & Molnar (2014) adopt, and the clearest single record of why the anuran names are false friends.

sources.authors: Reilly SM, White TD
sources.title: Hypaxial motor patterns and the function of epipubic bones in primitive mammals
sources.role: Hypaxial motor patterns in Monodelphis, and the epipubic bone as the link between the abdominal wall and the femur. A skeletal element this dataset does not yet carry.

sources.authors: Richardson MK
sources.title: Theories, laws, and models in evo-devo
sources.role: Conceptual review of homology, models and laws in evo-devo. Framing for how this dataset states homology hypotheses; not a source of anatomical records.

sources.authors: Russell AP, Bauer AM
sources.title: The appendicular locomotor apparatus of Sphenodon and normal-limbed squamates
sources.journal: Biology of the Reptilia 21 (Morphology I), pp. 1-465. Society for the Study of Amphibians and Reptiles
sources.role:
The lepidosaur limb monograph, and the source this corpus has been reading second-hand: Abdala & Diogo, Burch and Diogo & Molnar all cite it for the lizard and tuatara columns. 465 pages, of which pp. 192-394 are myology — general principles, then forelimb, then hindlimb, muscle by muscle — plus Appendix B, a synonymy list of the locomotor muscles that is the single most useful table in the bibliography for this project's `synonyms` fields.

**Its descriptive baseline is *Iguana iguana*.** Every muscle account opens with a paragraph keyed `Iguana:` giving that animal's origin and insertion, and only then a `General discussion:` surveying the literature — 74 such paragraphs across about 65 muscles. `iguana-iguana` carries 7 rows today, so nearly the whole appendicular musculature of a named, already-present lizard is in this file. *Sphenodon* is named 114 times but in the discussion paragraphs, reporting Perrin, Osawa, Miner and Haines rather than a dissection of the authors' own, so tuatara rows must be attributed to whoever observed them. Nothing here belongs to *Timon lepidus*, which is Abdala & Diogo's exemplar and carries 27 of the 36 unscored lepidosaur rows: this acquisition opens a second column rather than closing that one. Where it describes the tuatara it is the only source in the corpus that does, and `sphenodon-punctatus` has been in species.json with zero rows waiting for it. Where it generalises across squamates it is a clade statement, not a specimen, and rows taking it that way say so rather than borrowing Abdala & Diogo's *Timon lepidus*.

Acquired page-by-page from the Gans Collections and Charitable Fund's free release at carlgans.org; only the myology pages and Appendix B were fetched, not the whole chapter.

sources.authors: Sánchez HL, Rafasquino ME, Portiansky EL
sources.title: Comparative anatomy of the forearm and hand of wildcat (Leopardus geoffroyi), ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) and jaguar (Panthera onca)
sources.role: Felid forearm and hand. The cat is the animal most North American comparative anatomy labs put in front of students, and until now the therian forelimb rows came entirely from a mustelid.

sources.authors: Schilling N
sources.title: Evolution of the axial system in craniates: morphology and function of the perivertebral musculature
sources.role: Primary source for the axial muscle records. Reviews epaxial and hypaxial organisation across craniates, mapping character states onto a phylogeny, with fibre-type and activation data.

sources.authors: Schlough K
sources.title: Mustelid dissection guide
sources.role: Laboratory dissection vocabulary for the mink/ferret. Scanned images with no text layer, so it cannot be extracted automatically.

sources.authors: Schreiweis DO
sources.title: A comparative study of the appendicular musculature of penguins (Aves: Sphenisciformes)
sources.role: Penguin fore- and hindlimb myology. The most derived avian wing in the collection, and a useful contrast to the flight-adapted condition in Matsuoka & Hasegawa (2007).

sources.authors: Schumacher G-H
sources.title: The head muscles and hyolaryngeal skeleton of turtles and crocodilians
sources.journal: Biology of the Reptilia 4 (Morphology D), Academic Press, pp. 101-199
sources.role: Turtle and crocodylian cranial myology in one source, over ~40 chelonian species including *Pseudemys scripta*. **Written as a clade-level synthesis, not a species description** — the form is 'in all turtles X, and (Emys, Testudo, trionychids) Y' — so its rows belong on `testudines-generalised` for the same reason Werneburg's do, and it cannot close the species-level turtle cranial gap. Free from the Gans Collections and Charitable Fund.

sources.authors: Sefton EM, Bhullar B-AS, Mohaddes Z, Hanken J
sources.title: Evolution of the head–trunk interface in tetrapod vertebrates
sources.role: Developmental origin of the cucullaris / trapezius complex and the head–trunk muscle boundary.

sources.authors: Sigurdsen T, Green DM, Bishop PJ
sources.title: Did Triadobatrachus jump? Morphology and evolution of the anuran forelimb in relation to locomotion in early salientians
sources.role: Anuran forelimb and pectoral girdle function, including landing-force muscles.

sources.authors: Springer VG, Johnson GD
sources.title: The gill-arch musculature of anguilliform fishes
sources.role: Branchial arch musculature in eels. Outgroup detail for the branchial constrictor and levator records.

sources.authors: Starry A, James HF
sources.title: Anatomical atlas and three-dimensional musculoskeletal model of the flight apparatus in the southern screamer (Anseriformes: Chauna torquata)
sources.role: 3D atlas and musculoskeletal model of an anseriform flight apparatus. Check before scoring: a musculoskeletal MODEL is a different kind of source from a dissection, and this corpus already carries two (Allen et al. 2021, Hutchinson et al. 2015) whose rows could not be scored for exactly that reason. The atlas half may be scoreable where the model half is not.

sources.authors: Stephenson A, Adams JW, Vaccarezza M
sources.title: The vertebrate heart: an evolutionary perspective
sources.role: OUT OF SCOPE for this dataset — cardiac muscle, not skeletal. Listed so the papers/ folder is fully accounted for.

sources.authors: Tomańska A, Stawinoga M, Szturo K, Styczyńska M, Klećkowska-Nawrot J, Janeczek M, Goździewska-Harłajczuk K, Melnyk O, Gębarowski T
sources.title: Biological significance of the Komodo dragon's tail (Varanus komodoensis, Varanidae)
sources.role: Caudal musculature and its function in a large varanid. Companion to Kępa et al. (2023) and Tomańska et al. (2025); together the three cover forelimb, hindlimb and tail.

sources.authors: Tomańska A, Stawinoga M, Gębarowski T, Janeczek M, Klećkowska-Nawrot J, Goździewska-Harłajczuk K, Dobrzyński M
sources.title: The musculoskeletal anatomy of the Komodo dragon's hindlimb (Varanus komodoensis, Varanidae)
sources.role: Varanid hindlimb myology. Companion to Kępa et al. (2023) on the thoracic limb and Tomańska et al. (2024) on the tail. Descriptions are functionally framed rather than tabulated, so attachment extraction is partial.

sources.authors: Vanden Berge JC
sources.title: Notes on the myology of the pelvic limb in kiwi (Apteryx) and in other birds
sources.role: Avian pelvic limb myology with a ratite at its centre. Aves is the largest open clade gap at ~40 unscored rows and its scored rows skew neognath, so a kiwi is both new data and a corrective to the sampling.

sources.authors: Vélez-García JF, Carrión Blanco DA, Moreno Gómez G, San Martín Cañas S
sources.title: Descriptive study of the intrinsic muscles of the shoulder and brachium in kinkajou (Potos flavus) and an evolutionary analysis within the suborder Caniformia
sources.role: Shoulder and brachium of an arboreal procyonid, with the comparison drawn across Caniformia. The therian forelimb rows here come entirely from one mustelid (Ercoli et al. 2014); this is the second caniform that would show which of those rows are therian and which are Galictis.

sources.authors: Walker WF Jr
sources.title: The locomotor apparatus of Testudines
sources.journal: Biology of the Reptilia 4 (Morphology D), Academic Press, pp. 1-100
sources.role: The descriptive turtle limb myology the corpus never had. Type species *Pseudemys scripta elegans* — the red-eared slider, now *Trachemys scripta elegans*, which is the animal this dataset already used as its Testudines exemplar. Origin and insertion in prose for the pectoral, arm, forearm and hand series, compared against new dissections of Testudo graeca, Geochelone elephantopus, Trionyx spiniferus, Caretta caretta, Lepidochelys kempii, Pelomedusa subrufa and Chelodina longicollis, plus a per-muscle synonymy back to Bojanus (1819-21). Free from the Gans Collections and Charitable Fund; 212 attachment statements over 100 pages.

sources.authors: Walthall JC, Ashley-Ross MA
sources.title: Postcranial myology of the California newt, Taricha torosa
sources.role: Muscle-by-muscle dissection of the trunk, forelimb and hindlimb of Taricha torosa, with an origin and insertion stated for every muscle. The densest single source of attachment data for Caudata in this dataset, and the reference that lets the salamander column be scored bone-by-bone rather than inherited. Table 1 synonymises forelimb muscles across seven salamander genera and seven earlier authors.

sources.authors: Werneburg I
sources.title: The cranial musculature of turtles
sources.role: Source of the turtle cranial muscle records (his Appendix 1: 94 muscular units with origin, insertion, function, innervation and an exhaustive synonym list).

sources.authors: Werneburg I, Maier W
sources.title: Diverging development of akinetic skulls in cryptodire and pleurodire turtles: an ontogenetic and phylogenetic study
sources.role: Ontogeny of the turtle skull and its jaw musculature; complements Werneburg (2011) with developmental sequence data for cryptodires and pleurodires.

sources.authors: Werneburg I, Preuschoft H
sources.title: Evolution of the temporal skull openings in land vertebrates: a hypothetical framework on the basis of biomechanics
sources.role: Biomechanical framework linking temporal fenestration to jaw adductor volume, orientation and loading — the osteological correlate side of cranial muscle reconstruction.

sources.authors: Westphal N, Mahlow K, Head JJ, Müller J
sources.title: Pectoral myology of limb-reduced worm lizards (Squamata, Amphisbaenia) suggests decoupling of the musculoskeletal system during the evolution of body elongation
sources.role: Amphisbaenians retain all seventeen shoulder muscles regardless of how far the girdle and limb are reduced, but insertions shift onto connective tissue while origins stay ancestrally placed. That is this dataset's own thesis stated as a result — the muscle field is conserved while its attachments are the labile part — and it is the strongest available test of scoring attachment separately from presence.

sources.authors: Widrig KE, Bhullar B-AS, Field DJ
sources.title: 3D atlas of tinamou (Neornithes: Tinamidae) pectoral morphology: implications for reconstructing the ancestral neornithine flight apparatus
sources.role: Palaeognath pectoral morphology in 3D, framed explicitly as a reconstruction of the ancestral neornithine flight apparatus. The palaeognath half of the avian pectoral question, against Fisher & Goodman's neognath.

sources.authors: Winterbottom R
sources.title: A descriptive synonymy of the striated muscles of the Teleostei
sources.journal: Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia 125: 225–317
sources.role: The standard synonymy for teleost striated muscle — 93 pages reconciling competing naming schemes. The single richest untapped source of synonyms for the search index, and the reference that makes actinopterygian muscle names tractable.

sources.authors: Wiseman ALA, Bishop PJ, Demuth OE, et al.
sources.title: Musculoskeletal modelling of the Nile crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus) hindlimb: effects of limb posture on leverage during terrestrial locomotion
sources.role: Crocodylian hindlimb model with attachment coordinates and moment arms. The hindlimb counterpart to Klinkhamer et al. (2017) on the forelimb.

sources.authors: Zaaf A, Herrel A, Aerts P, De Vree F
sources.title: Morphology and morphometrics of the appendicular musculature in geckoes with different locomotor habits (Lepidosauria)
sources.role: Fore- and hindlimb muscle morphometrics in a ground-dwelling and a climbing gecko. Architecture data for a lepidosaur column that currently has none, and a within-clade functional contrast.

sources.authors: Zhu H
sources.title: Plastron reduction and associated myology in turtles, and its implications for functional morphology and natural history
sources.role: Turtle plastron reduction and the muscles that follow it. Unpublished thesis; the skeletal claim is the checkable part.

sources.authors: Ziermann JM, Diogo R
sources.title: Cranial muscle development in the model organism Ambystoma mexicanum: implications for tetrapod and vertebrate comparative and evolutionary morphology and notes on ontogeny and phylogeny
sources.role: Cranial muscle development in the axolotl, including muscles that appear in ontogeny and are lost at metamorphosis. Developmental evidence for the salamander cranial series, where the dataset is coarsest.

sources.authors: Ziermann JM, Diogo R
sources.title: Development of head muscles in fishes and notes on phylogeny–ontogeny links
sources.journal: In: Johanson Z et al. (eds), Evolution and Development of Fishes. Cambridge University Press, ch. 10
sources.role: Developmental origin (arch identity) and innervation of gnathostome head muscles.

sources.authors: Ziermann JM, Miyashita T, Diogo R
sources.title: Cephalic muscles of cyclostomes (hagfishes and lampreys) and Chondrichthyes (sharks, rays and holocephalans): comparative anatomy and early evolution of the vertebrate head muscles
sources.journal: Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society 172: 771–802
sources.role: Deep outgroup polarity for cranial muscle homologies (mandibular, hyoid, branchial arch series).

sources.authors: Cunningham DJ
sources.title: Report on some points in the anatomy of the Thylacine (Thylacinus cynocephalus), Cuscus (Phalangista maculata), and Phascogale (Phascogale calura), collected during the voyage of H.M.S. Challenger in the years 1873-1876; with an account of the comparative anatomy of the intrinsic muscles and the nerves of the mammalian pes
sources.journal: Report on the Scientific Results of the Voyage of H.M.S. Challenger, Zoology 5, part XVI: 1-192
sources.role:
**The dataset's first marsupials.** Theria was a placental column — *Homo*, *Rattus*, *Galictis*, four cats — and `monodelphis-domestica` sat in `species.json` carrying no rows at all. Cunningham dissected the thylacine, the spotted cuscus and the red-tailed phascogale, muscle by muscle, with origin and insertion for each and a running concordance against Macalister, Owen, Meckel, Haughton, Young and Cuvier & Laurillard's plates for the wombat, koala, Tasmanian devil, kangaroos, bandicoot and opossum.

The fore limb is complete in all three animals. **The hind limb is complete in only two**: Cunningham says plainly that the pelvis and hind limbs of the *Phascogale* arrived so shattered with shot that he could not examine them, so that animal has no hindlimb row here and the absence is a fact about the specimen, not about the muscle.

Its second half is a comparative survey of the intrinsic muscles and plantar nerves of the mammalian pes across some two dozen feet — monotreme, marsupial, carnivore, edentate, ungulate, rodent, bat and primate — which is where its platypus and echidna rows come from, and the only dissection in this bibliography that puts monotreme and marsupial foot muscles on the same page.

**Mined: 243 rows across 27 species** — 153 from the limb myology of the three principal animals, 90 from the pes survey. That is the largest single-source pass this dataset has had. Nineteen species entered `species.json` for it.

**It is a Victorian source and its names are Victorian.** Muscles are given human names — supinator longus, extensor secundi internodii pollicis, anconeus internus — and the mapping onto this dataset's comparative records runs through the human column, which is exactly what the human column was added for. Where Cunningham's own homology call differs from the record he lands on, the disagreement is in the row's note, attributed to him.
